articles.headline: Inadequate cholera vaccine worrying: Minister
articles.summary: Zimbabwe's Health Minister Douglas Mombeshora warned that cholera vaccines are inadequate to meet needs amid a regional outbreak that has infected over 200,000 people and caused more than 3,000 deaths in southern Africa. In Zimbabwe, since February last year the outbreak has yielded over 20,000 cases across all 10 provinces, with 452 confirmed deaths and about 300 suspected deaths. The country was allocated 2.3 million doses; about 892,000 have arrived and begun distribution. A further batch of more than 500,000 was expected around February 5, with doses released in batches until roughly 3 million are reached. The government aims to reach 7.5 million doses to meet the target. WHO and UNICEF are coordinating fair distribution. A district-focused prioritisation targets the most affected areas rather than constituencies; Zambia faces similar shortages with about 3 million doses.

articles.headlineTranslated: Funding Shortages Threaten Global Tuberculosis Control.
articles.summary: Funding shortages threaten global tuberculosis control as of March 19, 2026. The Deutsche Lepra- und Tuberkulosehilfe (DAHW) in Würzburg warns that shrinking financial support, especially from the United States, could stall progress against TB. The USA has historically funded roughly half of international TB financing per WHO, but last year this support was sharply cut. Without adequate funding, many countries cannot sustain essential testing and treatment. Projections indicate up to 11 million additional TB cases and up to 2 million additional deaths over the next five years. Zambia, Cambodia and Malawi are particularly affected due to dependence on US aid. WHO’s 2025 targets—to cut new infections by 50% and deaths by 75%—are at risk as 2024 financing stood at about $6 billion of the $22 billion needed. In Germany, 2024 TB cases were ~4,400; worldwide in 2024 about 11 million infections and 1.2 million deaths; treatment cures around 90%. Tuberculosis Day on March 24 highlights ongoing fight.

articles.headline: WHO calls for increased investment, leadership to end TB in Africa - The Nation Newspaper
articles.summary: WHO Africa region requires about $4.5 billion annually for an effective TB response, but faces a $3.6 billion funding gap, with an estimated 600,000 people undiagnosed or untreated each year. In 2024, TB killed 378,000 people in the African Region and infected 2.7 million, accounting for about one-quarter of the global burden; every 83 seconds a TB death occurs in the region. Despite the burden, progress is evident: TB deaths declined 46% between 2015 and 2024, and incidence fell 28%, with South Africa, Mozambique, Tanzania, Togo and Zambia meeting key global targets. Advances in diagnostics and shorter all-oral regimens for drug-resistant TB achieve cure rates above 85%. However, almost 70% of affected households face catastrophic costs, and many lack rapid diagnostic access. WHO urges sustained political will, greater domestic financing, national TB strategies, and empowered communities to end TB in Africa.

articles.headline: WHO: Africa Needs $4.5 Billion Annually To Strengthen TB Response
articles.summary: As of 2026-03-19, WHO says the African region needs US$4.5 billion annually for a comprehensive TB response, with a US$3.6 billion funding shortfall. Despite underinvestment, TB deaths declined 46% and incidence fell 28% from 2015 to 2024. Rapid rollout of six-month regimens for drug-resistant TB rose from near zero to about 40% between 2023–2024—the fastest uptake among WHO regions—and the six-month all-oral BPaLM regimen achieved >85% cure/success rates in Africa. Yet an estimated 600,000 people with TB are undiagnosed or untreated each year, and just over half of patients have access to rapid diagnostic tests; roughly 62,000 rifampicin-resistant TB cases occur annually. Milestones include South Africa meeting its 2025 incidence target; Mozambique, Tanzania, Togo and Zambia achieving a 75% reduction in TB deaths. WHO urges greater domestic funding, donor support, and community engagement to end TB.

articles.headline: TB kills every 83 seconds in Africa as 2.7m infected
articles.summary: TB kills every 83 seconds in the WHO African Region, where 2024 deaths reached 378,000 and 2.7 million people fell ill, about a quarter of the global burden. Between 2015 and 2024 deaths declined 46% and incidence 28%, with South Africa meeting its 2025 target and Mozambique, Tanzania, Togo and Zambia achieving a 75% reduction in TB deaths. The six-month all-oral BPaLM regimen now yields >85% success, and uptake among drug-resistant TB rose from near-zero in 2023 to ~40% in 2024, the fastest globally. However, about 600,000 people remain undiagnosed or untreated annually, and only just over half have access to rapid diagnostic tests; ~62,000 new rifampicin-resistant TB cases occur yearly. Economic costs are high, with ~70% of households facing catastrophic costs. Africa needs ~$4.5B/year but has a $3.6B funding gap. Urgent domestic investment, sustained funding, and community action are needed to end TB by 2027.

articles.headline: Zambia secures additional oral cholera vaccine doses
articles.summary: Zambia secured 586,730 additional oral cholera vaccine doses from the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision for deployment in identified high-risk districts to curb transmission and protect vulnerable communities. Details on targeted districts and implementation timelines will be announced once preparations are finalized. In 2026, the ministry vaccinated 189,920 people in hotspot areas across two Lusaka districts and Monze in southern Zambia; in 2025, nine districts were reached, with about 1.8 million people vaccinated. Cumulative cholera cases since fresh cases emerged last August total 1,267 with 21 deaths. The country’s worst outbreak occurred between October 2023 and July 2024, with over 23,000 cases and more than 700 deaths. Authorities are deploying a range of public health measures to interrupt transmission and contain the current outbreak.

articles.summary: As of 18 March 2026, Zambia reports a cholera outbreak with 13 additional cases in Lusaka and Mpulungu over the past 48 hours. The International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision approved over 586 additional cholera vaccine doses to bolster government efforts. Health Minister Alex Katakwe said public health interventions and strengthened surveillance will target high-risk areas for early detection and treatment, and urged the public to maintain good personal hygiene, treat drinking water, and seek medical care promptly if symptoms occur. The response stresses collective action to prevent transmission. At the same event, a new NHIMA board was unveiled, with Geoffrey Sakulanda as a board member, aiming to deliver inclusive, sustainable health services and resolve scheme challenges.

articles.headline: CICA intensifica acções de prevenção contra malária
articles.summary: Malaria prevention in Huambo, Angola, intensified in 2025 through the Council of Christian Churches in Angola (CICA) with the FLAME project—Advocacy by Religious Leaders for Malaria Elimination. At a training session, CICA secretary Pastor Euclides dos Santos said FLAME mobilizes believers to reduce mortality by distributing medicines, long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs), and other antimalarials, in partnership with NGOs and the government. The initiative also aims to assess and pursue malaria-control solutions across African countries and sent religious leaders to Zambia in November 2025 to learn from malaria vaccine results, noting Zambia has two doses of the vaccine. The program includes enhanced health education on prevention, sanitation, correct net use, elimination of standing water, and home fumigation with herbal methods. In 2025, approximately 974,902 people were affected by malaria nationwide, with 879 deaths in Huambo (case fatality rate 0.9%).

articles.headlineTranslated: Africa-United States Health Agreements: The Virologist's Warnings
articles.summary: At the end of February 2026, the United States signed 18 bilateral health agreements with 18 African countries totaling $19.8 billion (US pledges $12.2B; recipient nations $7.5B). Participating states include Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, DRC, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Uganda. Virologist Oyewale Tomori warns that conditions demanding rapid sharing of sensitive health data and pathogen samples—potentially for up to 25 years—risk sovereignty and access to resulting vaccines and therapies. The deals propose five-year initial terms but raise concerns about 20+-year data/pathogen sharing; critics urge locally funded capacity building and data control. Zambia’s health agreement is linked to a separate mining-sector deal; Nigeria’s accord emphasizes promoting Christian health providers with about $200M for 900+ facilities, sparking inclusivity debates. The package aims nearly $2.1B for HIV, TB, malaria, maternal/child health, and polio, with Nigeria increasing national health expenditure by roughly 3 trillion naira.
